claims.text: Reducing oxygen and nitrogen impurity levels will improve high-temperature yield-strength retention in TiVNbTa-based refractory high-entropy alloys.
The improvement from reducing oxygen and nitrogen will occur by suppressing impurity-induced phase segregation.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will preserve room-temperature mechanical performance.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will leave alloy density largely unchanged.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during aging at 700°C.
Thermal-aging-induced segregation depletes solute interstitials from the metal matrix and produces progressive softening.
High-purity starting materials and inert-atmosphere processing will minimize oxygen and nitrogen contamination during fabrication.
Impurity control will produce a more uniform BCC solid-solution microstructure.
Impurity control will reduce segregated regions and secondary phases during high-temperature exposure.
Segregated regions or secondary phases act as weak spots during high-temperature exposure.
Suppressing interstitial-driven segregation will preserve beneficial solid-solution strengthening during thermal exposure.
Lower impurity levels will not adversely affect room-temperature ductility or yield strength.
The high-purity alloy will retain a yield strength above 800 MPa at 700°C.
The high-purity alloy will have room-temperature mechanical properties similar to those of a conventionally processed control.
TiVNbTa is an RHEA with superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis acknowledges that oxygen and nitrogen provide initial solid-solution strengthening, yet also asserts that reducing those interstitials will preserve beneficial solid-solution strengthening and leave room-temperature yield strength unchanged. No compensating strengthening mechanism is provided to reconcile these statements.
